specAnchors.text: CORE PRACTICAL 8 Analysis of some inorganic and organic unknowns.

primer.text: Unknown ions confess under the right witnesses. This note runs the ammonium, carbonate and sulfate test-tube reactions with their ionic equations and observations, then turns to the flame, where a cleaned wire and a single ion paint the colour that names the metal.

modules.title: Test-tube identification and the ammonium test
modules.opening: Core Practical 8 identifies unknown ions with nothing but test tubes and reagents. The ion menu covers ammonium, halides, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates and sulfates, and the ammonium test pairs sodium hydroxide with warm, damp red litmus that turns blue in ammonia's presence.
keyPoints: Simple test-tube reactions identify ammonium, halide, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and sulfate ions.
Solid samples are dissolved in deionised water before testing.
The ammonium test adds sodium hydroxide to the sample and warms it gently in a water bath.
Ammonia gas is released, and damp red litmus paper held at the tube mouth turns blue.
The ionic equation is NH4+ plus OH- giving NH3 and water.

low.restatement: Dissolve the solid, add alkali, warm the tube in a water bath and hold damp red litmus at the mouth: blue litmus certifies ammonium ions through the ammonia they release.
low.analogy: A handshake you can smell: the alkali squeezes ammonia out of the ammonium ion, and the litmus paper is the sniff-test witness that changes colour.
low.examPointer: State both the overall and ionic equations, and specify damp red litmus, not any paper, when writing the method.

medium.restatement: The alkali converts ammonium ions into ammonia molecules; warming drives the gas out of solution, and ammonia's basicity is what flips the damp red litmus to blue - the moisture on the paper lets the gas dissolve and act.
medium.analogy: Persuading a shy guest out of a room: the alkali nudges the ammonium ion, the warm bath opens the exit, and the litmus greets the guest in the doorway.
medium.examPointer: Explain the dampness requirement - dry paper cannot dissolve the ammonia, so the colour change needs the wet surface.

modules.title: Carbonate and sulfate tests
modules.opening: Carbonates announce themselves with fizzing and milky limewater, sulfates with a white barium precipitate. This lesson writes both ionic equations, runs the delivery-tube set-up for the carbon dioxide, and explains why acid comes first in the sulfate test.
keyPoints: Carbonate ions react with acid to release carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
The carbonate ionic equation is 2H+ plus CO3 2- giving CO2 and H2O; hydrogencarbonate releases the same gas one proton at a time.
The delivery tube carries the gas into a second tube holding limewater, calcium hydroxide solution.
Sulfate ions with acidified barium chloride give a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Hydrochloric acid is added first in the sulfate test to remove carbonates that would otherwise precipitate and confuse the result.

low.restatement: Add acid to the unknown: fizzing plus milky limewater convicts a carbonate; for sulfates, acidify first, then add barium chloride and read the white precipitate as the verdict.
low.analogy: Carbonates confess loudly by bubbling; sulfates need their own witness, the barium, and the acid clears the courtroom of carbonate impostors first.
low.examPointer: Write both ionic equations and state the acid-first rule with its reason when explaining the sulfate method.

medium.restatement: The limewater verdict is a precipitation chain: carbon dioxide converts calcium hydroxide solution into insoluble calcium carbonate, hence the milkiness; in the sulfate test the acid pre-treatment eliminates carbonate ions that would also form white barium carbonate, so any white precipitate that remains is sulfate's own.
medium.analogy: An alibi check: the acid removes the suspect (carbonate) whose fingerprints would match the crime scene's white powder, leaving sulfate with no cover.
medium.examPointer: Quote both the carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ionic equations, noting the proton ratio difference.

modules.title: Flame tests for metal ions
modules.opening: Metal ions paint a Bunsen flame in their signature colours. The technique is small: clean the wire until it shows no colour, touch the sample, and read the flame's edge. Cleanliness is everything, because a contaminated wire mixes colours and misleads the identification.
keyPoints: Metal ions heated strongly in a flame emit characteristic colours that identify them.
The nichrome or platinum wire loop is dipped in concentrated acid and held in the blue flame until no colour shows, cleaning it.
Cleaning prevents contamination, since mixed ions give mixed colours and ruin the identification.
The sample is held at the edge of the blue flame, avoiding letting the wire glow red-hot.
Each metal ion carries its own flame colour, listed in the flame-test colour table.

low.restatement: Acid-dip the wire, burn it clean, load a trace of sample, and hold it at the flame's edge: the colour that blooms there names the metal ion, provided no stray ion shares the stage.
low.analogy: A spotlight on a solo performer: any leftover performer from the previous act blends costumes and confuses the audience, so the stage is cleared first.
low.examPointer: Describe the cleaning step and the glow-red avoidance when writing the flame-test method.

medium.restatement: The emission is atomic: heat promotes electrons in the metal ion, and the light they emit falling back is the element's optical fingerprint; two metals together superimpose their fingerprints, which is why a single-ion sample is the method's precondition.
medium.analogy: Two radios on one frequency broadcast a jumble; one metal ion per flame keeps the broadcast clean.
medium.examPointer: Explain contamination as mixed emissions rather than a chemical reaction between the ions.

glossary.definition: Calcium hydroxide solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide as insoluble calcium carbonate forms.
Identification of a metal ion by the characteristic colour it emits in a hot Bunsen flame.
The equation showing only the reacting ions, such as the carbonate or sulfate test equations.
